claims.text: A machine-learning regression model can be trained using defect-inclusive simulations and experimental conductivity measurements for bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The training data can include HfNbTaTiZr specimens containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Machine learning can capture relationships among defects, temperature, and material mechanisms over a wide temperature range.
Machine-learning interatomic potentials have been used to study defect-related mechanisms in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Defects and incorporated oxygen act as temperature-dependent scattering centers that alter electron-transport paths in HfNbTaTiZr.
Quantum and impurity scattering effects dominate the electrical conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr from 0 to 200 K.
Phonon scattering predominates in HfNbTaTiZr from 300 to 1200 K.
Experimental conductivity measurements from 300 to 1200 K exist for HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Conventional analytical conductivity models for HfNbTaTiZr are based on perfect, defect-free crystals.
Conventional perfect-crystal analytical models neglect scattering from defects and oxygen impurities.
Including defect structures, oxygen concentration, and temperature correlations will produce more realistic conductivity predictions than perfect-crystal analytical models.
The machine-learning model will outperform conventional analytical models for bulk HfNbTaTiZr in both specified temperature regimes.
The model will predict electrical conductivity within ±20% of experiment throughout 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Model applicability is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with defect structures represented in the training data and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen for the high-temperature case.
Accuracy may degrade for extreme impurity concentrations or fabrication processes not represented in the curated data.
Inadequate representation of real microstructural variability may cause systematic prediction errors.
Deviation by more than 20% from measured conductivity at any tested temperature in either regime for the oxygen-containing specimen would falsify the hypothesis.
The benchmark compares the machine-learning predictions with measured conductivity and predictions from existing analytical models.
